blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: An LP with 12 rows is solved twice: once by dual simplex, once by barrier with crossover switched off. In one answer 9 variables sit strictly between their bounds; in the other, 31 do. Which answer has 31, and why?

options.text: The simplex answer, because simplex stops once it is inside the region
options.says: Simplex moves along edges between vertices and stops on a vertex, which has at most one in-between variable per row: at most 12 here.

options.text: The barrier answer, because it nears the optimum from inside the region
options.says: Right: barrier approaches the optimum through the interior; crossover is what moves it to a vertex, and here it is off.

options.text: The simplex answer, because dual simplex leaves some rows broken at the end
options.says: Dual simplex repairs broken rows until none is left; its final answer satisfies every row and sits on a vertex.

options.text: The barrier answer, because barrier rounds its variables onto their bounds
options.says: Barrier keeps away from the bounds until the end; it does no rounding, which is why its raw answer has many in-between variables.

origin.section: Interior Point Crosses the Inside in a Few Expensive Steps

questions.stem: A national grid study has an LP with 60 million nonzeros. Barrier runs out of memory while factoring, and simplex is still pivoting after a day. The planners need an objective within 0.01% and do not need a vertex. What do you try next?

options.text: GLOP's primal simplex, as its pivots are cheaper than a factorization
options.says: Simplex is already too slow on this model; switching to another simplex form does not change what each pivot has to maintain.

options.text: HiGHS's barrier with crossover, as crossover lowers its memory use
options.says: Crossover runs after barrier finishes; it does not shrink the factorization that ran out of memory.

options.text: PDLP, as each iteration only multiplies the matrix by a vector
options.says: Right: a first-order method needs no factorization, and a 0.01% target is well within what it reaches.

options.text: HiGHS's dual simplex, as dual simplex skips the rows it cannot repair
options.says: Dual simplex repairs every broken row before it stops; it skips nothing, and it is still a simplex method.

origin.section: PDLP Takes Many Cheap Steps and Stops Within a Tolerance

questions.stem: A CI test solves a cost-minimizing LP on HiGHS and on PDLP, both OPTIMAL. HiGHS returns 8,410,226.31 and PDLP 8,410,229.05. The test asserts the two values are equal, and fails. What should the test check instead?

options.text: That the gap divided by the larger value is at most 1e-6
options.says: Right: the gap is about 3.3e-7 of the value, inside PDLP's tolerance; the check scales with the objective's size.

options.text: That the two values agree once rounded to whole numbers
options.says: These two round to different whole numbers, and any two values either side of a rounding boundary do, however close they are.

options.text: That the gap between the two values is at most 1e-6
options.says: An absolute 1e-6 on an objective of eight million asks for more accuracy than PDLP's tolerance gives, so correct runs fail.

options.text: That PDLP returns the lower value of the two, as it minimizes
options.says: Either solver may land on either side of the true optimum within its tolerance; neither is promised to be lower.
